title: CVDI Human Disease Portal Methods
bodyHtml:
Meta-analyses v1 (PMID: 39210047)

We assembled results from three large biobanks with sequencing data (see Figure 1). We performed gene-based testing of 9 masks using mixed-effects models, and performed a meta-analysis across the datasets. Of the 9 masks, 6 represented ‘rare variant’ masks where qualifying variants had to have MAF<0.1% across continental ancestries; 3 masks represented ‘low-frequency’ masks where variants with MAF<1% across continental ancestries were included (Figure). Masks consisted of different combinations of loss-of-function (LOF) and/or missense variants (Figure). Prior to meta-analyses, we removed mask-phenotype results with cMAC<10 in a dataset (please note that results with <20 distinct alternative allele carriers were removed in All of Us, as per sharing policy). To account for potential sample overlap between All of Us and MGB, we applied a Z-score based meta-analysis as implemented in METAL. After meta-analyses, we combined the P-values from each mask into a single P-value using the Cauchy distribution test (see Figure 1). Please consult the associated manuscript for the in-depth methodology regarding analyses and meta-analyses.

Figure 1.

 

Meta-analyses v2 (unpublished)

We assembled results from three large biobanks with sequencing data - UK Biobank, All of Us Research Program (V8), and Massachusetts General Brigham Biobank (see Figure 2). In each dataset, we constructed disease phenotypes from ICD codes using the PhecodeX library (https://github.com/PheWAS/PhecodeX), requiring >=1 inclusion code for a given phenotype, and requiring at least 100 cases for a phenotype to be included in the analysis (leaving 2,697 unique Phecodes across the three datasets).

We then performed rare variant gene-based association testing, using whole-genome ridge regression models with approximate Firth's corrections to account for case-control imbalance (REGENIE V4.1). We then performed a meta-analysis across the datasets, using an fixed-effects inverse-variance weighted approach to compute meta-analytical effect sizes, and using a count-based saddle-point-approximation to compute meta-analytical P-values (again, to better account for miscalibration due to imbalance) (see https://github.com/seanjosephjurgens/UKBB_200KWES_CVD for more details). We analyzed 24 masks (i.e. combinations of rare variants), composed of 8 different variant annotations (2 loss-of-function [LOF], 2 missense, and 4 LOF+missense combinations) and composed of 3 different frequency cutoffs (population maximum minor allele frequency [MAF]<0.1%, MAF<0.001%, and MAF<1%). As such, 16 tested masks are composed of 'rare variants' only (MAF<0.1%), while 8 masks are inclusive of 'low-frequency' variants (MAF<1%). Note that, prior to meta-analyses, we removed mask-phenotype results with cumulative minor allele count <10 in a dataset (please note that results with <20 distinct alternative allele carriers were removed in All of Us, as per sharing policy); after meta-analyis, we removed results with cumulative minor allele count <20.

After meta-analyses, we combined the P-values from each mask into a single P-value using the Cauchy distribution test (see https://github.com/seanjosephjurgens/UKBB_200KWES_CVD for more details), resulting in a consolidated gene-disease P-value. In this manner, we computed a single Cauchy P-value for each gene-disease association using only 'rare variant' results, and a P-value inclusive of both 'rare' and 'low-frequency' results (see Figure 2).

Figure 2.

 

Effect sizes

For all associations, effect sizes are on the log(Odds Ratio) scale. For mask-phenotype pairs with some minimal level of association (at least P<0.05 in a dataset), we re-estimated effect sizes using an approximate Firth’s bias-reduced logistic regression, to account for case-control imbalance. Then, mask-phenotype effect sizes were meta-analysed using an inverse-variance weighted fixed-effects meta-analysis. Generally, the point estimates for mask-phenotype pairs are highly robust to case-control imbalance. However, it should be noted that standard errors are not corrected for case-control imbalance. We therefore strongly recommend that users utilize the P-value and the effect size point estimate for reporting. NOTE: If investigators want to use summary statistics for other approaches (ie meta-analysis with other datasets) the same applies, although accurate standard errors may be estimable from P-value and effect size. Users may reach out to sjurgens@broadinstitute.org for more information/guidance.
